lines: Jordan Lee
+1 (555) 010-2468 | jordan.lee@example.com | example.com/code/jordan-lee
EDUCATION
Western State University | M.S. in Computer Engineering | Metro City, USA | Sep 2024 - Expected Jun 2026
Eastern Institute of Technology | B.S. in Electrical Engineering | Metro City, Country | Sep 2018 - Jun 2022
EXPERIENCE
Eastern Robotics Co. | Junior Software Engineer | Metro City, Country | Aug 2022 - Jul 2024
- Owned the diagnostics service's monitoring dashboards across two major releases and the on-call rotation that used them.
- Reduced p95 API latency from 420 ms to 180 ms by adding a request cache and batching sensor reads, with load tests that fail the build if p95 exceeds 200 ms.
- Maintained the CI pipeline for the perception team's model releases, adding automated regression checks that shortened release cycles from 2 weeks to 3 days.

- Migrated 30 robot-fleet services from cron jobs to an event queue while rewriting the shared logging library, onboarding two new hires and taking over the weekend on-call rotation, which removed the nightly backlogs that delayed morning dispatch.
Mobility Systems Company | Machine Learning Engineering Intern | Metro City, USA | Oct 2024 - May 2025

- Built a diagnostics triage branch for an industrial inspection system that screens 800+ sensor signals per case with ML-extracted features, cutting the pending-case backlog 68% in the eight weeks after launch.
- Raised diagnostic accuracy on 1,200 held-out cases from 71% to 79% by fine-tuning a domain adapter on validated tool-use trajectories with assistant-only loss masking.
- Cut p95 latency of single-request edge inference by 40% by serving the INT8 engine with dynamic batching.
- Using grouped tool-use rollouts, a composite reward over accuracy, citation validity and call count, and a GRPO loop with a frozen SFT reference, reduced end-to-end latency 5%.
- Stabilised GRPO training on sparse rewards by sampling a single rollout per prompt, so each update used exactly one scored trajectory.
- Documented the triage branch's abstention rules and escalation paths for the on-call reviewers, who adopted them as the team's runbook.
PROJECTS
Agent Runtime Suite | Owner | TypeScript, Multi-Agent Systems | Aug 2025 - Present
- Drove adoption of AI-first engineering practices across the platform, accelerating delivery and improving outcomes for downstream teams.
- Cut p95 tool-call latency from 900 ms to 600 ms, a 50% reduction, by caching tool results and reusing completed sub-agent answers.
- Raised the runtime's task-completion rate by 12% on the benchmark suite, from 71% to 83%, by retrying failed sub-agent calls with their partial context.
Research-Agent Evaluation Framework | Contributor | LLM Evaluation | Feb 2025 - Jul 2025
- Upstreamed 8 citation and faithfulness metrics to an open-source research-agent framework, where they now run in the default benchmark for every release.
- Showed the evaluator tracks injected degradation with a Kendall correlation of 0.89 across 400+ report-level trials that removed citations, sources and claims.
- Traced 3 structural pipeline defects in stability, sourcing and parameter handling to their modules with layered instrumentation; each was fixed upstream.
SKILLS
Programming: Python, TypeScript, Git
ML & Agents: PyTorch, LoRA, GRPO, agent evaluation, Kubernetes

items.says: Put the experience entries in reverse chronological order, with Mobility Systems above Eastern Robotics.
items.because: The internship is more recent and more relevant to the ML-focused résumé.

items.says: Make the code link a live, recognizable professional profile or repository.
items.because: A generic landing page is less useful to recruiters.

items.says: Confirm the submitted phone number and email are real.
items.because: Placeholders are acceptable only for the review.

items.says: Keep the link clickable in the PDF.
items.because: Clickable links improve recruiter usability.

items.says: Confirm the expected graduation date against the official program timeline.
Consider adding strong, relevant academic details.
items.because: The degree alone does not yet explain the ML and agent focus.

items.says: Explain what was changed or maintained in the dashboards.
items.because: The ownership claim is vague.

items.says: Add the scope of the dashboard or on-call work.
items.because: Numbers of dashboards, services, alerts, incidents, or users would make the work clearer.

items.says: Add an operational result if possible.
items.because: Across two major releases describes duration, not impact.

items.says: Fix the forced line break in “on-call” in the final PDF.
items.because: A compound word should not split awkwardly.

items.says: Clarify the load-test conditions, especially volume or concurrency.
items.because: Latency numbers are more credible when the test environment is defined.

items.says: Check whether caching and sensor-read batching both materially contributed.
items.because: Otherwise, the wording implies equal causality without support.

items.says: Emphasize the automated regression work rather than “maintained.”
items.because: “Maintained” understates the contribution.

items.says: Specify what the regression checks validated.
items.because: The checks could cover accuracy, performance, safety, packaging, or deployment behavior.

items.says: Define what changed from two weeks to three days.
items.because: “Release cycle” could mean cadence, engineering lead time, or validation duration.

items.says: Split the bullet into separate migration and operational-leadership points.
items.because: It combines service migration, queue architecture, logging, onboarding, on-call work, backlogs, and dispatch impact.

items.says: Quantify the backlog or dispatch improvement if possible.
items.because: “Removed” is absolute and may invite questions unless the backlog reached zero.

items.says: Explain the event queue or fleet’s operating scale.
items.because: Migrating 30 services lacks operating context.

items.says: Consider identifying the internship as part-time if it was.
items.because: Its overlap with the master’s program could otherwise confuse recruiters.

items.says: Clarify what “branch” means.
items.because: It could be read as a source-control branch rather than a deployed workflow or component.

items.says: Define a “case” and give the starting backlog if permitted.
items.because: The scale behind the 68% reduction is not visible.

items.says: Explain or replace “ML-extracted features.”
items.because: It is too broad to communicate the technical contribution.

items.says: Substantiate attribution of the eight-week backlog reduction to the system.
items.because: Staffing or demand changes may also have affected the backlog.

items.says: Name the exact evaluation metric if it was not simple multiclass accuracy.
items.because: Diagnostic systems may call for recall, precision, sensitivity, or class-specific performance.

items.says: Clarify whether the 1,200 cases were a fixed, untouched test set.
items.because: It is unclear whether they were also used during tuning.

items.says: Specify the type of domain adapter if confidentiality permits.
items.because: The phrase does not say whether it was LoRA or another method.

items.says: Explain why assistant-only loss masking mattered, or omit it.
items.because: It should represent an important technical decision you can explain.

items.says: Consider reporting uncertainty or repeated-run consistency.
items.because: The eight-point gain may have been evaluated only once.

items.says: Reconcile “single-request” latency with dynamic batching.
items.because: Batching usually requires concurrent or queued requests, so the mechanism sounds contradictory.

items.says: State the inference benchmark conditions.
items.because: Hardware, concurrency, batch behavior, sequence size, and request volume affect the result.

items.says: Separate the effects of INT8 quantization and batching.
items.because: Otherwise, the claimed cause of the reduction is difficult to assess.

items.says: Define the latency measured by the 40% reduction.
items.because: It could mean model inference, service, or end-to-end latency.

items.says: Reduce the procedural detail before the result.
items.because: The sentence is dense and delays the contribution.

items.says: Explain how the composite reward reduced latency.
items.because: The connection is plausible but not explicit.

items.says: Give the latency baseline or absolute change.
items.because: A 5% improvement alone is comparatively weak.

items.says: Distinguish end-to-end latency from the earlier edge-inference result.
items.because: The 5% and 40% reductions currently sound duplicative.

items.says: Add a quality constraint if latency improved without harming quality.
items.because: The bullet does not say whether diagnostic accuracy or citation quality was maintained.

items.says: Use consistent comma style in the reward-component list.
Verify or correct the single-rollout GRPO description.
items.because: Standard GRPO uses multiple completions in a comparison group unless grouping occurred another way.

items.says: Define “stabilised” with a measurable indicator.
items.because: Variance, convergence, failed runs, or reward collapse would make stability concrete.

items.says: Explain why one scored trajectory improved sparse-reward training.
items.because: The causal claim is not intuitive as written.

items.says: Correct the algorithm name if the method was not standard GRPO.
Use “stabilized” for a U.S. application.
items.because: “Stabilised” is inconsistent with the requested American spelling convention.

items.says: Add the number or type of reviewers if meaningful.
Add evidence of operational impact if available.
items.because: The bullet does not show effects on escalations, review speed, or incident handling.

items.says: Clarify “branch” if it means a deployed triage path.
items.because: It could otherwise suggest source control.

items.says: Identify what kind of project Agent Runtime Suite is.
items.because: “Owner” does not establish whether it is personal, open-source, research, or internal.

items.says: Include a repository or demonstration link if public.
Give adoption scale if other people use the project.
Remove the bullet or add specific actions and measurable outcomes.
items.because: It has no concrete action, scope, or measurable evidence.

items.says: Substantiate any platform-wide influence.
items.because: The number of teams, users, workflows, or releases affected is not shown.

items.says: The reduction from 900 ms to 600 ms is about 33%, not 50%.
items.because: Numerical errors undermine trust in other metrics.

items.says: Define the benchmark conditions and cache hit rate if available.
Explain how reused sub-agent answers were validated or invalidated.
items.because: Changed context creates correctness risks.

items.says: Say whether the latency figure covers all calls or only cache-eligible calls.
The increase from 71% to 83% is 12 percentage points, not an unqualified 12%.
items.because: The relative improvement is approximately 16.9%.

items.says: Define the benchmark suite and number of tasks.
Say whether results used a fixed test set and whether retries increased latency or cost.
Clarify the maximum retry policy.
items.because: It should be clear the gain did not come from unlimited attempts.

items.says: Clarify the framework’s status and link to the project or contribution if public.
Verify that all eight metrics were accepted and remain in the default benchmark.
items.because: Continued default use should not be implied without confirmation.

items.says: Clarify whether you designed the metrics, implemented existing definitions, or both.
Specify the Kendall correlation variant if relevant.
Explain what was ranked or correlated.
items.because: The degradation types are given, but the exact comparison is not.

items.says: Report stability across repeated trials or degradation categories if known.
items.because: The reliability of the 0.89 result is otherwise unclear.

items.says: Explain the defects’ impact.
items.because: The bullet only labels them as stability, sourcing, and parameter-handling defects.

items.says: Clarify what “sourcing” means in this system.
Describe the debugging result more precisely than “to their modules.”
Link to relevant issues or pull requests if available.
items.because: They would support the upstream-fix outcome.

items.says: Git is listed as a programming language.
items.because: It is a development tool.

items.says: Consider adding SQL if you genuinely used it.
items.because: Many ML engineering roles screen for it.

items.says: Kubernetes is listed as an ML or agent method.
items.because: It belongs in a tooling, infrastructure, or cloud category.

items.says: Separate frameworks, training methods, evaluation methods, and infrastructure.
items.because: Recruiters could scan the skills section more quickly.

items.says: Keep GRPO only after resolving the experience bullet’s inconsistency.
items.because: You should be able to explain its objective, reference policy, grouping, and advantage estimation.

items.says: Order skills by relevance and strength.
Use consistent date separators and dash characters.
Keep dense bullets to roughly two lines where possible.
items.because: The migration and GRPO bullets are currently too dense.

items.says: Make metric denominators, benchmarks, and operating conditions clear throughout.
Keep the final layout one-column and ATS-friendly, with selectable text.
